references.text: Enoch walked with God, and he was no more, for God took him. This is the earlier example in Genesis of one who 'walked with God' (hithallek et ha-Elohim), the same expression used about Noah in 6:9.

The Lord said to Noah, 'Go into the ark, you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation.' This confirms Noah's righteousness 'in his generation' as described in 6:9.
God said to Abram, 'Walk before my face and be blameless (tamim).' The same key word is used as in the description of Noah: to walk with God and be tamim (blameless/wholehearted).

Even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were there, they would only save themselves by their righteousness. Noah is mentioned as a prominent example of a righteous man, consistent with the description in Gen 6:9.

By faith Noah was warned by God about things not yet seen, and in godly fear he built an ark to save his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.

God did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, along with seven others. Noah is referred to here as 'a preacher of righteousness,' which expands on the description of him as a righteous man in Gen 6:9.

They were disobedient in Noah's days, while God waited patiently as the ark was being built. In it, a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water. The context shows Noah's situation in his generation.
The verses show the connection between Noah's character as righteous and his concrete obedience in carrying out God's commands.
Proverbs formulates a theological principle about righteousness for which Noah's life in Genesis is the concrete historical fulfillment.
